title: Restriction zone scheme for offenders to start in October
description: A scheme that could see serious sexual and violent offenders confined to areas just a few miles wide after leaving prison will be launched in October,
body: A scheme that could see serious sexual and violent offenders confined to areas just a few miles wide after leaving prison will be launched in October, Justice Secretary Alex Norris has announced.Government ministers say this is designed to give victims greater freedom and further reduce the possibility of unwanted contactThe intention to introduce "restriction zones" for violent offenders who leave prison and who are on probation was first announced by the government last year.Probation officers will be able to limit where serious offenders can go for as long as it is deemed necessary. Those who breach their new boundaries could be recalled to prison.This would go beyond the current practice of imposing "exclusion zones" which ban offenders from specific locations such as a victim's home or place of work. Norris is expected to come up with proposals to further restrict the early release of some prisoners when Parliament resumes next month.But the Conservatives say that the best thing Labour could do to protect victims is to bring forward emergency legislation which would stop the early release of thousands of criminals.There is a risk that serious sexual and violent offenders and victims could encounter one another outside exclusion zones.The new scheme will specify confined areas for offenders in plans tailored to them and developed in consultation with victims.Norris said the scheme would use GPS technology monitored by probation officers so that "those who step outside the boundaries can be quickly identified and face being sent back to prison"."Offenders should carry the consequences of their crimes, not their victims," he added.Amy Glover, director of domestic abuse services at Advance, a charity supporting women and girls who have experienced domestic abuse, praised the "change in focus".However, she also called for reform to the criminal justice system saying many survivors of abuse chose "not to pursue a criminal conviction, and for those that do only 5% reach conviction."A domestic abuse survivor named only as Kristina called the restriction zones a "fantastic concept" but noted that a perpetrator had continuously breached her indefinite restraining order "without consequence"."The biggest challenge would be to gain victims' confidence in authorities to follow through their promises of protection," she added.The announcement of the restriction zone scheme's start date comes after a change to the government's early release scheme following a backlash.Introduced to ease prison overcrowding, on 4 August the policy was updated so people sentenced for rape, serious child sex offences and grooming would not be eligible for early release.The Prison Governors' association warned this change to plans at a "very late stage" put further pressure on prison staff.The restriction zone scheme was criticised when it was announced last year for potentially putting pressure on probation staff, something the government says it hopes to alleviate with more staff and a greater use of technology.If you are suffering from domestic abuse, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

schema.headline: Restriction zone scheme for offenders to start in October

title: Trump waves green flag at IndyCar race through Washington DC
description: Image source, ReutersByKwasi Gyamfi Asiedu and Helena Humphrey Reporting fromat the IndyCar fan zone in Washington DCUS President Donald Trump was amo
body: Image source, ReutersByKwasi Gyamfi Asiedu and Helena Humphrey Reporting fromat the IndyCar fan zone in Washington DCUS President Donald Trump was among hundreds of people who gathered to see the IndyCar race through the streets of Washington DC on Sunday, marking the culmination of a series of summer events to celebrate the country's 250th birthday.Driver Kyle Kirkwood won the race, earning his seventh career Indycar win.Ahead of the race, the president and First Lady Melania Trump took a ceremonial lap of the 1.7-mile track in his presidential limousine, The Beast.As they reached the finish line, Trump's new Air Force One completed a flyover above the capital.The Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the first time professional road racing has been hosted in the capital.Image source, ReutersImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Melania Trump waved to fans from the trackImage source, ReutersWith a maximum speed limit of 55mph (89kmh), Washington DC has the lowest speed limit in the United States. But on Sunday, some of the world's fastest drivers zoomed past the capital's famous monuments and museums at speeds of up to 190mph (306kmh).The 25 professional drivers competing in the event face 147 laps featuring seven crucial turns, making a total 250-mile course - a nod to the nation's anniversary.The drivers sped past the Washington Monument and museums on the National Mall, before passing a finish line with the US Capitol building in frame.Figure caption, The BBC's Helena Humphrey took a test drive of the track earlier in the weekSimilar to Formula 1, the IndyCar series is a road race featuring open-wheel, single-seater cars.But unlike F1, where teams design and build their own cars, the engines in IndyCars come exclusively from Chevrolet or Honda.Image source, ReutersOrganisers of the Freedom 250 Grand Prix say about 140,000 people are expected to attend, with many given free general admission tickets through a lottery.However, premium packages sold for $5,000 for a pair of passes.The event has been a huge logistical and security lift for the city, and has led to widespread road closures, manholes being bolted down, and road resurfacing.The Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, which primarily runs domestic flights, has been under a three-hour airspace closure to accommodate the US military flyover.Image source, Getty ImagesThe National Gallery of Art conducted vibration tests to ensure its priceless collection could withstand the powerful rumble of the engines.On race day, however, the roar of celebration appeared to largely drown out any irritation. Many of those lining the circuit were there after winning tickets through a public lottery. Some wore Uncle Sam hats, while one woman came dressed as the Statue of Liberty. Families had travelled from across the country for what they saw as a once-in-a-lifetime event.American driver Josef Newgarden told the BBC that the significance of racing through the capital was not lost on him."It's super unique. You might never see this again, and as an American driver, it's very special celebrating the 250th anniversary of the country," he said. "It's a beautiful city, and it's very surreal."In other events earlier this summer, Trump hosted an Ultimate Fighting Championship event on the White House lawn, as well as a fireworks show on 4 July.Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Driver David Malukas' car is carried out after crashingImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A pit stop for driver Felix Rosenqvist

schema.headline: Trump waves green flag at IndyCar race through Washington DC

title: Vietnam: Gen Z seek justice for teen killed in ex-politician's car crash
description: Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi.
body: Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi. Then the bouquets started piling up.It was here that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving his BMW in May last year when he veered into the opposite lane and smashed into a motorbike carrying a father and his teenage daughter.The father, Do Viet Hung, suffered a broken leg but survived. The daughter, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, died in hospital 10 days after the collision which severed her right leg.Fifteen months later, her death, and the silence surrounding it, has become a lightning rod for discontent among Vietnam's youth.In early August, a legion of anonymous social media users started publishing millions of posts with the hashtags #NguyenSyCuong and #BMW across Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X. The users identified themselves as Gen Z – and they demanded accountability.Initial discussions circled around whether the former politician was in fact the one who had caused the accident, and why authorities had only released sparse information.Some pointed to reports that the driver of the BMW had the initials NSC and was born in 1961, leading to speculation that he was a former member of parliament. Others claimed the incident had been swept under the rug due to the influence of powerful figures. Many reported that their posts had been deleted by social media platforms at the request of the Vietnamese government – providing screenshots of notifications as evidence. These claims could not be independently verified.Expressions of outrage and calls for a proper investigation grew in number, volume and force.Meanwhile, masked flower bearers started to appear, gravitating towards the scene of the incident and laying vibrant bouquets at the base of what has now been dubbed the Justice Tree. Police quickly arrived to get rid of the flowers, prompting mourners to create a virtual equivalent of the tree online - where hundreds of thousands of people have since sent tributes and paid respects.Pressurised by more than a year's worth of growing suspicion and a rush of online attention, the issue had become too big to ignore. Then, last Monday, the government made an extraordinary admission.State broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV) televised an official statement from authorities, confirming what had happened on the day of the incident. Former National Assembly deputy Nguyen Sy Cuong was indeed driving his car down Nguyen Huy Tu Street on 30 May, 2025, when his vehicle suddenly swerved across the road and into an oncoming motorcycle.VTV cited police and prosecution sources who said that because Nguyen Sy Cuong "sincerely confessed and actively and fully remedied the consequences of his actions", Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's family had submitted a petition to exempt him from prosecution. The report did not specify what form this remedy took, but Nguyen Sy Cuong was cleared of all criminal liability.While such a decision is lawful under Vietnam's legislation, lawyers have questioned whether the criminal proceedings were conducted in accordance with due process – or conducted at all. Social media users were quick to highlight his political connections and call for a more thorough investigation.Such online pressure had yielded results in the past.In March this year, a 66-year-old man driving under the influence of alcohol in Hanoi collided with seven other cars and three motorcycles in a chain-reaction crash that killed one woman and seriously injured two others.In the wake of that incident, it emerged that the driver, Nguyen Van Sau, was a retired police colonel who had previously served as deputy director of a department under the Ministry of Public Security. Fearing that the driver was not being held culpable, the victim's family appealed for help. Social media users in turn amplified the issue, and after three months Nguyen Van Sau was charged with "violating regulations on participation in road traffic".Many now feel that a similar groundswell may be the only way to deliver justice for the teenager who died last year. But their efforts have been met with friction.Do Viet Hung, the teenager's father, appeared in VTV's broadcast to thank internet users for their sympathy, but said the family was satisfied with the investigation's findings, and asked people to leave them alone. Notably, he also warned people "not to be drawn into the influence of reactionary elements".Also appearing in the broadcast was a senior police official, who suggested that people were leveraging the incident to stoke dissent.The Ministry of Public Security had "uncovered highly dangerous plots and intentions by hostile forces, reactionaries and bad actors to incite unrest and cause disorder", the official said."The ministry advises the public, especially young people, to remain fully alert and highly vigilant."Similar rebukes have also started emerging on social media, with some claiming that conspiratorial forces were manipulating young people in Vietnam to stoke political discontent, manipulate public opinion online and rally people in real life ahead of the country's national holiday on 2 September.Others have accused Gen Z Vietnamese of plotting a "colour revolution" – a term used to refer to mostly nonviolent protest movements that use specific colours or flowers as their symbol.This is a familiar line of critique from Vietnamese authorities, who have previously labelled people's grievances or resentments as being untrue, unreasonable, or stemming from information fabricated by some "anti-government" or "reactionary" organisation.Many in this case have said such accusations are baseless, insisting they are simply seeking justice for the victim of a fatal traffic accident. But the growing outrage has inevitably become a flashpoint amid broader, simmering grievances felt by Vietnam's youth.Despite the Vietnamese government's tightening control over people's online freedom of expression – through measures ranging from intimidation and fines to criminal prosecution – public opinion in some corners has started to swerve against the Communist Party line.On platforms such as Threads and Reddit, where anonymity is more normalised, many young people have expressed discontent towards various social issues: from the expansion of police power and land reclamation projects to exam cheating scandals and stricter regulation of online communication.Such grievances echo those condemned by other Gen Z-led movements across the broader Asia region.In countries like Bangladesh, India and Nepal, youth-led anti-government uprisings have over the past 12 months rallied immense support against the various pressure points of corruption, nepotism, economic inequality and democratic backsliding. Unofficially dubbed "the Asian Spring", the expanding influence of these movements has spread from Iran, Mongolia and the Maldives to the Philippines and Timor-Leste.But protests in Vietnam have rarely, if ever, reached such fierce extremes. Vietnamese authorities have historically proven effective at detecting and stifling dissent before it boils over into action. Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.Many are simply seeking justice for a teenager who was killed in a tragic accident, and accountability for a former lawmaker who appears to have been granted special clemency.Yet even the mere suggestion that this incident could foment an uprising has provoked alarm – along with harsh reminders of the longstanding status quo in Vietnam's one-party state."Are these Gen Z kids planning a colour revolution using this accident?" reads one widely shared post. "Are they trying to emulate Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, and then create an Asian Spring? Remember, this is Vietnam! This is not Nepal, India, or Bangladesh!"

schema.headline: Vietnam: Gen Z seek justice for teen killed in ex-politician's car crash

title: Doctors wrongly said I was too young to have endometriosis at 13
description: But the most frustrating thing for Grace, and why she contacted BBC Your Voice, is because she does not feel medical experts recognise that teenagers
body: But the most frustrating thing for Grace, and why she contacted BBC Your Voice, is because she does not feel medical experts recognise that teenagers and adolescents can suffer from endometriosis.Grace's GP did not diagnose her condition and nor did the first consultant she saw privately.She says: "Even a specialist didn't believe me. And if a specialist won't listen to me, who will?" It was not until the family pushed for a second private opinion that she got a positive diagnosis.Endometriosis, which occurs when tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows outside it, can cause debilitating symptoms, such as pelvic pain, heavy periods and fatigue.  About 10% of women are affected by it, according to NHS data.This week BBC presenter Emma Barnett revealed she had to have a hysterectomy for her endometriosis - which she said she never wanted to have. It can develop at any age once periods begin - and it is a common misconception that only older women suffer from the condition, says the charity Endometriosis UK,Faye Farthing, a spokesperson for the charity, says the government, NHS and health practitioners need to improve menstrual health education for young people "if we are to ensure the next generation are not robbed of the future they deserve".The charity says it can take a long time to diagnose endometriosis - an average of nine years in older women. And in the early stages, for example with teenagers, it often doesn't show up on an ultrasound scan. However, new tests are being developed which will help spot the condition earlier.Getting pregnant can be more difficult - even aged 14, Grace says she has been warned it is likely to affect her fertility. She's been advised she may not be able to have children after the age of 30 because of damage to her reproductive organs. She feels rushed: "I have to have kids within the next 15 years, otherwise I might not be able to."Paediatric gynaecologist Dr Gail Busby says nearly 80% of adolescents will have painful periods, but clinicians should recognise when a patient's symptoms are not normal - like missing school, missing PE every month or not going out with friends. She says: "When you're in bed and your best friend is a hot water bottle - that's not normal."Grace's case, showing symptoms at the age of 13, is not unusual, says Dr Busby, who sees girls both younger and older than Grace at her clinics. As well as her NHS work, she has opened a private adolescent endometriosis clinic in Manchester.The impact of symptoms is not just physical. Girls like Grace are more likely to suffer with anxiety or depression because their pain affects what is an important time for educational, emotional and social development."We should enjoy adolescence," Dr Busby says, "but they can't do what they enjoy doing, what their peers are enjoying doing."There is a history of endometriosis in Grace's family, but her mum Samantha says that did not make it any easier to get a diagnosis."When your child's on the floor in pain, it's very clear it's not just a bad period. But professionals say 'Oh we'll just put you on the pill for six months and see see how we go.'"Grace has recently had a laparoscopy - keyhole surgery - to remove her endometriosis. She hopes the procedure will help relieve her symptoms, at least temporarily. She has been advised to take a hormonal contraceptive to help slow monthly tissue growth and lessen the pain.By speaking out, Grace hopes more teenagers will have the confidence to pursue a diagnosis. "I felt I was going crazy. That it was all in my head," she says. "But actually, you know your body best and your pain is real."

schema.headline: Doctors wrongly said I was too young to have endometriosis at 13

title: Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse
description: US President Donald Trump has said Canada wants "the benefits of being a State, without being one" after trade talks between the two countries collaps
body: US President Donald Trump has said Canada wants "the benefits of being a State, without being one" after trade talks between the two countries collapsed late on Friday.His comments come after negotiations broke down, triggering new 50% US tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, Trump also said American farmers had been charged "massive amounts of Tariffs" for years.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the fresh tariffs a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us".Carney confirmed he would match Trump's tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, including levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The US and Canada are now in a trade "war", he said."They asked too much and they offered too little," Carney said on Saturday. "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he added.Trump's latest comments echo his repeated references to making Canada the "51st state" of America since returning to office, sparking frustration among its leaders and residents.The collapse of the trade talks upended a deeply integrated trading relationship, with no clear path to resolution."We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said.On Sunday, while speaking to Fox News, Trump said the Canadians were "foolish" to engage in a trade war with the US and think they will "actually win".Both countries were optimistic of a deal earlier in the week, but talks fell apart after both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes.The new 50% US tariffs will apply to a range of Canadian goods, in addition to existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.They are limited in scope, covering about $20bn (£15bn; C$28bn) of Canadian imports, or about 5% in total, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.The prime minister said Canada was retaliating "reluctantly" to protect its interests. Details of the counter-measures will be released in the coming days, he said. Leaders of other federal parties in Canada, including the Conservative opposition, voiced support for the prime minister, as have the leaders of some Canadian provinces.Tariffs - a tax placed on imports from other countries - have been a key component of Trump's trade policy, with the US president arguing they will boost American manufacturing and create jobs at home.Critics, however, say tariffs have raised prices for American consumers and have disrupted and damaged the global economy.Carney's speech on Saturday was his first address to Canadians after he announced late on Friday night that a deal would not be reached, accusing the Americans of making "last-minute changes" that were "unfair" and "uneconomic". US negotiators, meanwhile, accused Canada of making "new demands and walk backs" on terms which had been previously agreed.On Saturday, US trade representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News there were no plans to resume talks.He added that the US had been prepared to cut some of its tariffs on Canada as part of the ill-fated deal.Carney, however, said the US presented "unacceptable" terms that were too restrictive, including curbing Canada's ability to strike new trade deals with other countries.He also rejected the assertion that Canada had made last-minute requests: "We clarified what was on offer and were continually disappointed by the answers."Doug Ford, the leader of Canada's most populous province Ontario, backed Carney and said Trump "can't be trusted". British Columbia Premier David Eby said the US demand for restrictions on Canada's ability to have other trade deals "would reduce us to the economic equivalent of the 51st state"."It was never acceptable to Canadians," Eby said. The Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre also appeared to support Carney, calling the latest US levies "unjustified".Quebec's premier, Christine Fréchette, warned jobs would likely be lost as a result of the new US tariffs."Behind these numbers are real people," she said, vowing to introduce measures to support impacted sectors.Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, whose oil-rich province has worked to make inroads with the Trump administration, urged both sides to resume talks.The collapse comes after more than a year of on-again, off-again trade talks, which intensified in recent weeks after a US-imposed deadline to strike a deal or face further tariffs.The two countries were also engaged in a mandatory review of an existing North American free trade agreement, known as USMCA, with Mexico. The pact was signed by Trump during his first term to replace the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement. It underpins $1.6tn (£1.2tn) in annual trilateral trade across Canada, the US and Mexico. Earlier this summer, Canada and Mexico had formally requested for USMCA to be renewed for another 16 years. The US, however, declined to renew it in its current form.Asked how Friday's trade talk collapse would impact the North American free trade pact, Carney said it was "certainly not good news".

schema.headline: Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse

title: Brydon Carse: What will it take to prevent England from more hangovers
description: Yet again, the England men's cricket team is picking through the wreckage of a late-night misdemeanour. The latest stain on the game's reputation is a
body: Yet again, the England men's cricket team is picking through the wreckage of a late-night misdemeanour. The latest stain on the game's reputation is a result of pictures of fast bowler Brydon Carse in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers outside a nightspot in Derby. His Durham team-mate Matthew Potts is in the images, while former England captain Ben Stokes appears in the background.If you're keeping score, we're now up to eight England players involved in incidents of this kind since Halloween last year.Harry Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington, with Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue present. Ben Duckett was filmed drunk in Noosa, then Stokes and Gus Atkinson were there when a member of England's security staff was struck in a London nightclub in June, breaching a curfew in the process.To put it another way, there are 30 men currently on England central contracts. More than a quarter of them have been caught up in bother in the past 10 months. Of the four separate incidents, two have involved punches being thrown and another was a police matter.In Carse's case, the time spent in handcuffs came days after new England Test captain Joe Root called on his players to be "really good role models, good human beings".Root was speaking the day before England's first Test against Pakistan, for which Carse was part of the squad. The match was scheduled to still be ongoing when he found himself in the hands of the police.It is understood that Carse was not arrested. Both the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) and the Cricket Regulator will work to establish what happened. There are early suggestions he was denied entry back into a nightclub, or he had a drink poured over him.Carse was also not specifically on England duty at the time. He was released from the first-Test squad to play for Durham away at Derbyshire and was scheduled to report to Lord's for the second Test on Monday.As of Sunday evening, he remains part of the squad for the second Test. England will take time to gather some information before a decision on his involvement is made.Root warned his squad to "be adults" when he abolished the midnight curfew - in his first act as captain - that came into place after previous incidents. As part of that move, guidelines advising players about not drinking alcohol on the day before, during or after a game, or in public, have also been removed.There is a duty of care towards Carse. Two years ago, the 31-year-old was banned for historical betting offences and rebuilt his career to become an England regular in all three formats. No bowler has more Test wickets for England than Carse's 58 since he made his debut in October 2024.But there is also a deep sense of anger and frustration within the ECB at having to deal with another error of judgement by a high-profile player. Supporters will take their own view, among them a sense that the behaviour of these players is now beyond parody.Does someone have to be left out of a squad or given a meaty suspension for the penny to drop? This might be the opportunity for Root to stamp his authority on a new era.Naturally, there will once again be the debate about not denying players their freedom or stopping them from enjoying a victory.For Carse, a Saturday night out came less than 48 hours before he is scheduled to report for England. He is only a tweaked hamstring away from playing in a Test at Lord's on Thursday.Perhaps more damning is the kind of trouble this group of England players seem to find. Two punch-ups and a set of handcuffs. It also does not appear to have dawned on them that they are high-profile individuals, likely to attract attention, with footage finding its way to social media, as happened with Carse.And what about Stokes, who, despite being retired, remains an employee of the ECB via his central contract.As the former captain, should Stokes have been conscious about Carse being in that situation? What about the trouble in which Atkinson found himself alongside Stokes in June?Three weeks ago, Stokes denied the England team has a drinking culture, but rather that the game itself has a problem. What has Stokes done to distance himself or those around him from that drinking culture?Now there is a wait to see what happens next. The ECB only became aware of the incident on Sunday afternoon. The governing body will take a breath overnight and decide if Carse needs to be removed from the Test squad.Perhaps, on Tuesday, director of cricket Rob Key will once again explain why the players he manages cannot keep themselves out of trouble. In the aftermath of the Stokes-Atkinson incident in June, Key denied that England have become a "national embarrassment". He may be asked again.Key also might be asked about the whereabouts of new Test coach Stephen Fleming, who does not take up his post until the winter. Might Carse have been less inclined to step out of line had the new sheriff been in town?Well, here is another situation for England to manage. Only strong action will ensure there are no more.

schema.headline: Brydon Carse: What will it take to prevent England from more hangovers

title: Norris and McLaren 'don't have car' to fight for title
description: Lando Norris says he and McLaren "don't have the car I need to fight for a championship", despite a second consecutive win to open the second half of
body: Lando Norris says he and McLaren "don't have the car I need to fight for a championship", despite a second consecutive win to open the second half of the Formula 1 season.The Briton's victory in the final Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, following on from his first win of the season in Hungary last month, was of the highest calibre. As such, it raises the prospect of the sort of championship fightback staged by Red Bull's Max Verstappen against Norris himself last year.After this race last year, Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri had a 34-point advantage over the Briton and 104 over Verstappen. Yet Verstappen, after one of the all-time great fightbacks, finished the season just two points behind Norris as he won the title in Abu DhabiNorris' masterful victory in Zandvoort has left him 83 points off the lead, held by Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, who he and McLaren passed on track after losing the lead at the chaotic start of the day.Antonelli's team-mate George Russell is tied on points with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, 59 behind the Italian.But while McLaren have made a major step forward with upgrades to their car that led to convincing wins in both Hungary and now the Netherlands, Norris believes that the car still has too many flaws to mount the sort of consistent attack Verstappen produced last year."I'm confident because we clearly have a strong car," he said. "We have a strong car in certain areas. It's not like last year where we were pretty good everywhere."We're very, very strong in high speed, and that's the place we've improved the car the most, is high-speed performance. No one matches us in high speed, and that's a good thing."My pace advantage to Mercedes in Turn Seven, Eight was crazy, but their advantage that they have to us in slow speed is also crazy."And therefore, I don't have the confidence to say, 'Yeah, I can easily fight for a championship for the rest of the season.'"I know I've just won two races in a row and had two poles in a row, but at the minute I don't have the car I need to fight for a championship. And I know that's quite a big comment."Norris' belief is based on his understanding that McLaren's slow-speed performance will be a handicap at the next race in Monza, and two races after that in Azerbaijan.Both tracks are dominated by long straights, which penalise the McLaren's high drag compared to Mercedes, and have very few high-speed corners where the car's strength can compensate for its weaknesses in slow turns.McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: “If we can confirm our improvements in Monza, then we can look with some optimism at the remainder of the season.”Norris' victory in Zandvoort, built around an off-set strategy and devastating pace once the cars were on the hard tyres in the second stint, underlined the level at which he is now operating.As impressive as Verstappen's revival was last year, Norris' own in the second half of the season was almost as good, as both made up ground on Piastri.And Norris believes he has built on the progress he made in his driving after a difficult start to 2025 to perform on an even higher plane in 2026."I was driving at a high level the second half of last year," he said. "It's tough to say, but I do think it's a trickier car to drive this year in some ways. And I think you can see that because the gaps between team-mates are often bigger this year, I would say, than it was last year."I do believe I'm able to understand situations better, to understand the car in a better way. It's still just horrible to drive, but I'm doing a better job at just understanding this, relaying this to my team, figuring stuff out."So, it's not just I'm driving better on track. I'm certainly eliminating my weaknesses on track, and I don't have so many, but it's also how I work off the track. And for me, yesterday to today is a perfect example of the work we put in overnight transformed our race and gave me the opportunity to win."Team principal Andrea Stella said he believed Norris was driving better than ever."Lando is driving and operating at a very high level," Stella said. "He's driving at the level of a world champion."What I like the most of his journey in Formula 1 is that he keeps improving."After the start of the 2025 season, something clicked, which is not only a single click, but it's a way of working with Lando, for Lando, and that we are adopting also on Oscar's side now in particular."This approach has led Lando to continuous improvements."It's almost like I see Lando stronger and stronger race by race. Because I think this weekend was nowhere near a weekend in which we could fight for the victory for granted, especially after having seen the performance in the sprint (in which Norris was passed by Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and finished third)."But we invested in trying to understand where was the opportunity from a tyre exploitation point of view and car improvement."And then when you have conditions in which the car slides in the race, there's not much grip, then I think he is the master in these kind of conditions."A couple of months ago, before the British Grand Prix, and before McLaren had won a race this season, Norris admitted in an interview with BBC Sport "a little bit" of frustration at not being able to defend the title he won last year.So it's perhaps no surprise that now he appears to have at least an outside chance of making a fist of it, he is not making any presumptions."One race at a time," he said. "I know a lot of people say it now, but it's the truth of it. There's no point thinking that far ahead."Obviously, two great weekends, but there's still plenty of things we can do better, and we need to do better if we want to fight for a championship."It's still harder than I would like, and I don't want a bigger gap, so we have to keep working hard. There's still plenty of races, plenty of opportunity for everyone. So, keep my head down, keep working, and they'll keep coming."McLaren's progress has come in the context of stagnation at Mercedes, whose lack of an upgrade to their car since Canada in May has led to them being caught by McLaren and Ferrari, a situation that has raised eyebrows among rival teams.The next Mercedes upgrade is not due until the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in four races' time.For Antonelli - who also faces a grid penalty at his home race in Italy next time out because he needs to take a new engine that exceeds his allowance as a consequence of early-season reliability problems - it cannot come soon enough."Now as a team we need to find a little bit of time because McLaren have done a huge step," he said."So for sure, in this race, it's going to be more difficult, it's going to be challenging, but we're ready to do our best and to maximise every opportunity."And then hopefully it's going to be our turn to bring the package that's going to give us a little bit of the upper hand again."

schema.headline: Norris and McLaren 'don't have car' to fight for title

title: Wicker Man director's sons complete their late father's film trilogy
description: Image caption, Dominic and Justin Hardy embraced the legacy of their father's film The Wicker ManByScotland arts correspondentRobin Hardy always envis
body: Image caption, Dominic and Justin Hardy embraced the legacy of their father's film The Wicker ManByScotland arts correspondentRobin Hardy always envisaged his iconic 1973 folk horror film The Wicker Man as the first part of a trilogy.The Wicker Tree, released in 2011, brought him closer to that ambition, but his death in 2016 at the age of 86 left the project incomplete.Now his sons, Justin and Dominic, have been able to complete their father's trilogy, after finding a script for the final film.Wrath of the Gods has its premiere at the FrightFest horror festival in London, external on Friday, a family dream made possible thanks to the surprise discovery of some long-lost family archive."The person who bought Justin's old family home said they'd discovered six sacks of letters, scripts and other material pertaining to Robin Hardy and The Wicker Man in the attic," says Dominic, an art historian at the University of Quebec in Montreal."Justin's first instinct was to burn them, but we couldn't ignore this original source material. Although we left it unopened for six months or more."The archive haul included papers, scripts and storyboards, but it also shed light on the long shadow cast by The Wicker Man. The film holds a unique place in British cinema history. It was shot at a time when the UK industry was in crisis. Its financial backers were struggling and its stars - including horror legend Christopher Lee - had to go without being paid to get it finished.It was set on a Hebridean island in spring but was shot in Galloway in the autumn and early winter. On its release, it was largely buried as a second feature. There were competing edits and tales of missing material, some of which was said to be literally buried in the supporting columns of a motorway.But the film's reputation grew. Lee considered it one of his finest films, featuring one of his finest performances. Its off-kilter tone and genuinely disturbing climax made it a favourite for horror fans.By the time the BBC launched the cult cinema series Moviedrome in 1988, external, there was only one choice for opening night - the premiere of a previously unseen edit of The Wicker Man.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Wicker Man itself was built on a cliff in GallowayImage source, Robin KeaneImage caption, Wrath of The Gods draws on Viking and Shetland mythologyThe film's troubled production was mirrored by the troubles it brought Robin Hardy and his family.It bankrupted the director, and he abandoned Justin's mother Caroline, leaving her with all his debts.He went on to marry four more times, and had eight children in all.Justin and Dominic talk about their complicated relationship with the film in the 2024 book and documentary Children Of The Wicker Man.The recently unearthed archive included a script for that proposed third and final film, Wrath of the Gods, as well as details of how their father had come up with the idea."He had had been in an airplane and had a turn because his heart medication wasn't working," says Dominic."He had to land in Reykjavik and spend a week recuperating, and he came back with this idea of a theme park around an extinct volcano in Iceland where the Norse gods get upset and mayhem ensues. "And then he decided it ought to be set in Shetland because of the other parts of the trilogy."Justin, an Emmy and BAFTA-nominated director, worked on the idea with Dominic. They came up with their own original story, in which a young grieving widow returns to the island of Hel to bury her late husband after his suicide. She's cast out by the community, who look on her as a symbol of evil and bad luck. When children start going missing, the island is forced to confront its own complex history.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Justin Hardy (left) was one of his father Robin's eight children, including sister ArabellaImage source, Hardy PicturesImage caption, Justin and Dominic Hardy worked through their late father's archiveFilming began in Shetland in the spring of 2025.While the two leads are played by Game of Thrones and Rose of Nevada actor Francis Magee, and Norwegian actress Christiane Schaldemose, the rest of the cast was found locally."It feels like a huge honour," says Lynsey Rendall, who plays Francis's screen wife Maeve."The Wicker Man is such a famous film and has such an impact on popular culture so it was amazing to be part of that world."John Haswell has worked in theatre for a number of years but says his role as the Rev Knox was a highlight of his career."He's a sleazy man of the cloth and I had an absolute ball working on it," he says. "It was an intense six weeks, filming in Voe virtually every day. It wasn't glamorous but that's part of the fun."Martha Robertson is 17-years-old and was sitting her Highers during filming. She says the experience helped her launch a career in acting."There was one scene we filmed which was meant to be in the pouring rain on a dark gloomy day but it fell on what seemed to be the sunniest day of the year," she says."They had to black out all the windows and two crew members were on a wall with a hose and a leaf blower so we could get wind and rain."Which seemed really crazy because it rains every day on Shetland, but not the day we needed it to."Image caption, Lynsey Rendall, John Haswell and Martha Robertson are among the locals who joined the cast of Wrath of The GodsImage source, Hardy PicturesImage caption, Director Justin Hardy died just before the film's premiereMany of the Shetland cast and crew plan to attend the premiere of Wrath of the Gods at the horror festival FrightFest in London on Friday.But their celebrations have been overshadowed by the sudden death of Justin Hardy last month at the age of 61."We all were – still are – looking forward to seeing the finished film," says John."But now it's not just a celebration of the film, it's a celebration of Justin and his life. It will be wonderful and sad. A complex mixture of emotions."For Lynsey, the film is a testament to the late director."It was such a massive risk," she says."So to get to the end of that process, when it's going to be on a screen, feels a bit miraculous really and it's so vexing that Justin isn't going to be there to see what he so passionately wanted to achieve."For the Hardy family, it has become a strange tribute to three of their number.Wrath of The Gods completes Robin Hardy's Wicker trilogy and is dedicated to Justin's mother Caroline, who was a secret uncredited executive producer on the original 1973 film. She died in 1984, aged 51, without knowing that the film she'd backed would go on to be so loved and admired."It will be poignant beyond imagining. A sad but celebratory moment," says Dominic."I know that he [Justin] was extremely proud of it being taken by FrightFest."Justin's efforts have brought us all together as a family and helped us harness all our energy."

schema.headline: Wicker Man director's sons complete their late father's film trilogy

title: Newcastle 2-2 Liverpol: Relief for Andoni Iraola but Liverpool have work to do
description: When Liverpool came to Newcastle last August, there was utter jubilation as Rio Ngumoha scored a remarkable 100th-minute winner.They scored late again
body: When Liverpool came to Newcastle last August, there was utter jubilation as Rio Ngumoha scored a remarkable 100th-minute winner.They scored late again this time around, through Dominik Szoboszlai's 99th-minute penalty, but it felt more like a sense of relief than joy as they rescued a point.Andoni Iraola said afterwards that his side did not deserve to lose and, to their credit, they never gave up as they earned a 2-2 draw. A defeat would have been Liverpool's first on the opening weekend since 2012-13. A draw will do wonders for their spirit but it will certainly not mask their concerns."It's probably not the result you want when you come in before the game but we definitely deserve this point and even more," Iraola told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The team has never given up and we've recovered one point and probably the taste is better because we score in the last minute."Iraola will be content with the outcome, given his side trailed twice at a raucous St James' Park.But on the flight back to Merseyside on Sunday evening, he would have had time to consider the performance, which highlighted why his squad needs more depth."You're expecting Liverpool to get top four this season at least but they didn't look like a top four team today," former Scotland winger Pat Nevin told 5 Live. "There are more players to come in, so you can't make a real decision on how their season is going to go."There's a definite lack of creativity and somehow they must get the best out of Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak because you certainly didn't get the best out of them today."All eyes were on Wirtz and Isak - the Sweden striker, signed from Newcastle in a drawn-out saga last September, was booed relentlessly whenever he touched the ball. Wirtz did start positively, but was replaced just after the hour mark after Newcastle went 2-1 up.Isak had 28 touches and looked fired up but wasted a brilliant opportunity in the second half - the kind of which he would take regularly when he was at Newcastle.Both of them, signed for nine-figure fees last summer, will know that their overall output and connection must improve over the coming weeks and months.This remains a Liverpool side offering more questions than answers. One significant question is the Cody Gakpo conundrum, which will roll into the final week of the transfer window. If Liverpool do bring in two more attacking players then Gakpo may leave.The club have been linked with Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye and have had two bids rejected for Brighton's Yankuba Minteh.Yet Dutchman Gakpo was Liverpool's best player at Newcastle and took his goal brilliantly - while there was another positive in the performance of Spanish forward Victor Munoz on his Liverpool debut from the bench. Munoz won the late penalty after replacing Ngumoha but Iraola's decision to take off the English teenager off after just over an hour summed up how much he struggled down the right.Ngumoha will turn 18 next week and has preferred to play down the left throughout his youth career but failed to have an impact on the other side.With Iraola determined to have his wingers able to play on both sides, it remains to be seen if that experiment persists once Liverpool get more attackers in. What is for certain is that Iraola needs more options. Once Munoz and Alexis Mac Allister came on in the 63rd minute, Iraola's remaining bench options were: Giorgi Mamardashvili, Ronald Araujo, Wataru Endo, Kostas Tsimikas, Trey Nyoni, James McConnell and Lewis Koumas. Defensively, both Milos Kerkez and Jeremie Frimpong had poor games at full-back and Liverpool were undone on the counter attack for both of the goals they conceded. The lack of a defensive midfielder showed and it was revealing to see Iraola use Mac Allister just ahead of the back four after Joe Willock put Newcastle 2-1 up.Liverpool have now conceded more goals via fast breaks in all competitions than any other Premier League team since the start of last season - nine.All that and more will be food for thought for the new Liverpool boss but this was a relatively positive start to life under Iraola - who prefers to wait until the day after the match for a debrief."I've liked a lot of the things I've seen from the team," he said. "There's definitely things to improve like the goals but I've seen a lot of things I've liked from the team. I've liked the energy, especially the players coming from the bench. I think we finished the game quite strong physically.""We will never give up. I can guarantee you that," Szoboszlai told Sky Sports. "We have to fight every time - all day long during the 90 minutes. Everybody who came off the bench also made an impact as well. We need the whole squad and we need to be ready."That desire was never a cause for concern on Tyneside. But this Liverpool squad must improve, both in terms of quality and quantity.

title: PCs killed in wrong-way A66 crash were heroes, say families
description: Two police officers who died when a car travelling the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle have been hailed as heroes by thei
body: Two police officers who died when a car travelling the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle have been hailed as heroes by their families.PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough on Saturday.The Passat's occupants - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.In tributes released by Cleveland Police, PC Clough's family said he had been "willing to help anyone", while PC Blades' wife described him as "loved beyond words"."No words will ever feel like the right words to honour our Matt," she said, adding that he had been a "beloved husband" and the "most devoted father" to their two young sons who would grow up knowing what an "incredible" dad he had been. "He gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness," she said."The pain of losing him is beyond words, and our lives will never be the same."Neither will the love he gave us ever fade."He may have left this world committed to the duty he believed in, but his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave to his family."She ended the tribute to her husband: "Forever loved. Forever missed. Forever our superhero. Our Matt and Dad."PC Clough's family said he had had a "fantastic sense of humour", jumping "into action whenever needed". They added that he had been their "hero", always "willing to help anyone for any reason".They also said he had "proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place" and had always been "on public duty throughout his short life".In other tributes, a man who had known PC Clough posted on social media that he had been a "true friend, fantastic soldier and I have no doubt even better police officer".Seaton Carew FC, where PC Blades had recently become a coach and was preparing for his first season with its under-sevens team, said the officer and his family were "much loved members" of the club.FC Hartlepool, where PC Blades had coached the under-10s team, said he had been a "role model, mentor [and] friend" whom the children had "looked up to and admired"."His kindness, patience, and infectious personality made him loved by all who had the privilege of knowing him," the club added.Carmel College in Darlington, where PC Blades taught English before joining the police, remembered him as an "intelligent, kind and approachable teacher" who "gave generously of himself to the young people in his care".On Sunday evening more than £180,000 had been pledged for the officers' families in an online fundraiser set up by Cleveland Police Federation, who said the two officers had "paid the ultimate sacrifice in the line of duty"."They leave behind heartbroken loved ones who will struggle to come to terms with the loss of their loved one," the federation said, adding the organisation would support the families "at this unfathomable moment" with the money to be used "as they so wish". Earlier a group of police officers laid floral tributes at the police cordon on Eston Road.Some removed their hats and bowed their heads and took a brief moment of silence to remember their colleagues.They spoke briefly to other officers at the scene before leaving, with some hugging each other as they walked away.When someone dies following police contact, it is mandatory for the case to be referred to the IOPC.Its director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, said the watchdog recognised the "devastating impact" the crash had on Cleveland Police and the "wider policing community".He said: "We have obtained initial accounts of officers involved in the pursuit, the incident log and in-car footage of the incident."Work is ongoing to obtain additional material."IOPC investigators will continue to review and analyse all the evidence available to us."A video posted on a TikTok account believed to belong to Makai Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.BBC Verify analysed the one minute 34 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.

schema.headline: PCs killed in wrong-way A66 crash were heroes, say families

title: Mayors to get powers to overrule local councils on planning decisions
description: Mayors across England will be given new powers to overrule local councils on some planning decisions.The change would apply to proposals with more tha
body: Mayors across England will be given new powers to overrule local councils on some planning decisions.The change would apply to proposals with more than 150 homes, more than 15,000 square metres of commercial space or buildings over 30 metres.Mayors in 13 areas including Manchester, Liverpool, the West of England and the West Midlands will gain similar powers to Sir Sadiq Khan in London, who is already able to "call in" planning decisions. Housing minister Matthew Pennycook said the powers were an "essential part of the toolkit that mayors need to effectively deliver new homes and regeneration".The Conservatives questioned whether it was right for councils to lose the "ability to make planning decisions in their own communities". The powers will also be available to mayors in the Combined Authorities in North East England, South Yorkshire, West Yorkshire, York and North Yorkshire, Hull and East Yorkshire, Greater Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, East Midlands, and Tees Valley.   Paul Bristow, the Conservative mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, told BBC Breakfast that if he had local powers, he would approve "tomorrow" a couple of blocked schemes that he said would "get new homes built that families could move into and charge economic growth".Bristow said "it's not about overriding what local people want", but about developers and councils finding a compromise on projects instead of just saying no - which he believed the "perceived threat of intervention" would help.In London, where Khan already has the power to review decisions on certain developments, external, housebuilding has fallen in recent years. But Pennycook insisted the "call in" powers had helped the mayor "unblock strategic growth sites" in the capital. Bristow said if he had a similar local plan it would be "much more light touch" than London.In the 2024 general election, the Labour government promised to build 1.5 million homes in England by the end of the decade, but housebuilders have warned the target could be missed.Pennycook said the government was "absolutely determined to stick with that ambition". He acknowledged the target was "really stretching" but said nearly 180,000 children were in temporary accommodation and "any smaller target wouldn't be commensurate with the scale of the challenge". Bristow said the government has "no chance whatsoever" to meet its 1.5 million target."We need economic growth in this country, we need to get building and families need places to live, and at the moment, the planning system just isn't working."In addition to gaining the new "call-in" powers, mayors are set to be able to grant "up-front permission", which the government says will allow building to begin "without a developer having to apply".  A consultation on how the powers will work is due to be published next week. The government has sought to stress that local councils will continue to decide the majority of applications and that all decisions must still follow planning rules. It has also said mayors will get a "bigger say" over how housing funding is spent in their area, with the government directing national agency Homes England to focus on local mayors' priorities. New Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who served as mayor for Greater Manchester for nearly a decade, has repeatedly expressed his desire to transfer more powers to local mayors."Challenge does need to be made to local decision-making and actually it cuts both ways," he told the Sunday Times."Sometimes it's the other way round. It's the local authority putting forward something that's unacceptable in terms of the impact on the community. It's a two-way street."Last month, Burnham promised to give all mayors a share of income tax revenue, saying he wanted to "bring power home" to "every postcode". Earlier this week, he announced a secondment programme to send high-performing civil servants to work in mayoral offices. The approach has faced criticism from some in his own party and the Liberal Democrats, who fear it could create a "two-tier system" that discriminates against those areas that do not have an elected mayor.Responding to the new powers for mayors, Sir James Cleverly, the shadow housing secretary, said the government was "simultaneously stripping councils across the country of their ability to make planning decisions in their own communities, while making it easier to build traveller sites against local wishes".Sir James also suggested Labour mayors had failed to meet housing targets, adding: "The Conservatives are the only party with a plan to get Britain building and moving again with our plan to scrap stamp duty on the family home."Gideon Amos, the Liberal Democrat housing and planning spokesperson, said "taking powers away from communities and local councillors is taking powers away from local people"."Instead of silencing residents and handing mayors a blank cheque, the government should be empowering local councils with the resources to deliver genuinely affordable homes alongside the infrastructure to support them," he added.Mothin Ali, deputy leader of the Greens, said "more powers for mayors to direct local councils" was "more tinkering from the Labour government when local authorities continue to be forced by government into austerity budgets".Reform UK accused Labour of "centralisation in disguise", saying: "Westminster is stretching its tentacles outward instead of giving real power, resources and decision-making capabilities to devolved authorities."

schema.headline: Mayors to get powers to overrule local councils on planning decisions

title: Viral Cat in the Hat TikTok trend sparks fake videos and real fear
description: "He's so scary!" says 16-year-old Skye, recoiling at the mention of the Cat in the Hat.Viral images purporting to show a life-sized version of the Dr
body: "He's so scary!" says 16-year-old Skye, recoiling at the mention of the Cat in the Hat.Viral images purporting to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character on the streets after dark have sparked fear and confusion among teenagers. The posts, seen by millions, have convinced some young people that the character is real and that they might encounter it, prompting police forces in Ireland and the UK to issue statements confirming that the images and videos are fake."I was having a sleepover," Skye elaborates, "but everyone started watching Cat in the Hat videos. It was 3am. I wanted to go home. When I started walking down my friends' driveway, I got totally freaked out that the Cat in the Hat was going to jump out. I had to call my mum to pick me up."A quick scroll through TikTok reveals numerous accounts, many of them created in the past few weeks, sharing photos and videos of an elusive black-and-white feline wearing the famous, towering, crooked red-and-white striped hat.One post showing the original Cat in the Hat costume, accompanied by the caption "Help, what do I do?", has received 14.6m views in just three weeks.The comments add to the sense of frenzy, with followers asking, "Why is he taxidermied?" Others zoom in on parts of the costume and post conspiracy theories about Mike Myers, who played the character in the 2003 film, being trapped inside.Another popular account set up this week, posts videos of a real person dressed in a cat in the hat costume, dancing, with captions like "Kent I'm coming. lock your doors." Other users are sharing the videos, adding their own captions and locations across the UK.Many of the AI generated images have been centred on the Irish counties of Limerick and Wexford, where shaky videos purportedly showed the character wandering through the streets, causing alarm and confusion among residents.In Wexford, the local Gardaí (police force) quickly dismissed the sightings as fake and confirmed that the images had been generated using artificial intelligence.That has not stopped the pictures and videos from spreading online - along with unverified claims posted without evidence that the Cat in the Hat has been involved in violent assaults."I low-key wanna go meet him…" says 14-year-old Lily, who heard that the Cat in the Hat had arranged a "meet and greet", inviting local TikTok followers to come to the woods in Galashiels, a small town in the Scottish Borders.Her mother was horrified by the prospect."You are not going to meet anyone in the woods in the middle of the night!" she told her.There is a point at which viral dancing videos and AI-generated clips of the Cat in the Hat become something potentially more sinister, with real-world consequences beyond their impact on teenage imaginations.In England, South Yorkshire Police has denied social media claims that a 'killer Cat in the Hat' has been spotted. Posts about the alleged sightings have attracted hundreds of thousands of views on TikTok.There is also a fake Facebook post claiming to be from Yorkshire Police - no force with that name actually exists - and suggesting that the force is taking the rumoured sighting seriously.In response, a South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said: "If you do see posts online providing policing updates and advice, please check that they are from an official policing account. The cat is not out of the hat on this one… Please don't believe everything you read on social media."As with so many trends driven by TikTok, comedic reaction and spoofery is what will be appearing right now on many people's For You page.In recent days, depending largely on what your algorithm serves up, you may be seeing nearly as many people in Cat in the Hat costumes dancing to Beyonce as those stalking the streets. There are several jokey videos depicting police chasing human sized cats, and Scottish drag performer Ellie Diamond has issued a video declaring that she is not the Cat in the Hat killer. And Irish TikTok star Garron Noone said on one post that it should have been obvious it was a hoax "because even the most soulless, evil, vicious monster" would be "traumatised looking in the window of a Wexford person".Snapchat filters and images shared in group chats suggest that many teenagers - and those not so young - are simply having harmless fun with the trend.But some do remain perturbed, including another teenager in the Scottish borders, 16-year-old Ellie, who says: "I was so scared of him when I was little," Ellie confides. "Now it's like he's actually come to life to haunt me."Emily, a mother in Scotland, says the trend reminds her of the "Momo Challenge", a notorious internet hoax and digital urban legend. At the time, fact-checkers and authorities found no verified evidence linking the meme to children harming themselves, although the frightening images were still capable of causing distress."I'm not worried about my daughters, but there could be people with bad intentions who might take advantage of this trend to manipulate teenagers."For now, the evidence points not to a real, roaming Cat in the Hat, but to a rapidly evolving online story built from an auctioned film costume, people in costume, AI-generated material and unverified posts.Whether the claims began as a joke or were deliberately designed to frighten and manipulate, the advice from police is the same: pause before sharing, check the original source and date, look for confirmation from official police accounts, and treat invitations to meet strangers, especially at night or in isolated places, as a serious warning sign.The rapidly evolving trend terrorising or tantalising teenagers on TikTok across the UK and Ireland is a reminder that online fear can quickly spill into the real world.Additional reporting by John Hand

schema.headline: Viral Cat in the Hat TikTok trend sparks fake videos and real fear

title: How easy is it to find an NHS dentist? It depends on where you live
description: Cornwall, Devon and Northamptonshire have seen some of the biggest reductions in the number of practices offering NHS care. In Cornwall, more than a q
body: Cornwall, Devon and Northamptonshire have seen some of the biggest reductions in the number of practices offering NHS care. In Cornwall, more than a quarter of practices that previously offered NHS treatment have stopped doing so, making it one of the starkest examples of the shift away from NHS dentistry.The findings come as ministers have pledged to tackle so-called "dental deserts", but dentists say the current deal is not viable. Many have handed back their NHS contracts because to work is loss-making.In Somerset, fewer than one in five dental practices now offers NHS services. Alan, 83, who lives in the county, says he has given up trying to find an NHS dentist."I used to try, but getting a dental appointment anywhere near where I live would be impossible," he says.Alan has only one tooth remaining after the others "crumbled out over the years" and says he has had to adapt what he eats, although he jokes that he has perfected a way of eating Brazil nuts.Vivak Shah, who runs three dental practices in Northamptonshire, continues to offer NHS treatment but says it operates at a loss. He no longer takes on new NHS patients."Each year we struggle to decide what to do, and there is a limit to how much the private side can cover the NHS losses," says Shah.He warned that if practices stop providing NHS treatment, many patients could be left in pain or forced to seek help elsewhere in the health service, including hospital accident and emergency departments."A contract handed back in one town attracts little national attention on its own but repeated across the country for a decade it amounts to the quiet transformation of dentistry into a two-tier service," says Mark Dayan, head of public affairs at the Nuffield Trust."Access to dental care increasingly depends on what people can afford to pay and where they live."Jim Sykes is a dentist in Hexham. He handed back his NHS contract in 2024."It was a really hard emotional decision, but the NHS work was running at such a loss. I had to think of my team of staff and make it work," he says. Sykes asked if he could continue treating just children but was told he had to accept adults as well, or give up the NHS work."There has been a real breakdown in trust for me. Even if there was a new government offer, I would still be very nervous about entering a new NHS contract," he says.Sykes says that none of his friends in his graduating class in dentistry still works in the NHS. "My friends have gone private, retired or teach - any pathway to avoid NHS dentistry."Shiv Pabary, chair of the British Dental Association's General Dental Practice Committee, says the situation is "the direct result of choices made by successive governments". He warns that unless ministers "fix and fund NHS dentistry", more dentists could choose to reduce their NHS work or leave the service altogether.Overall dentist practice numbers have risen in England over the last decade."This is not a shortage of dentistry but a shortage of NHS dentistry," says Dayan. "Practices will need to be incentivised back into NHS work in the places where the NHS footprint has thinned most."While most parts of England recorded declines in practices offering NHS dental care, the reductions were smallest in North West London, the Black Country and North East London.North East London was the only area to see any increase during the period, recording one additional practice offering NHS treatment compared with a decade ago.Every other region of England saw the number of NHS dental practices fall.Looking at the number of practices doing NHS work is not the same as looking at exactly how much health service capacity there is - practices can vary in size. But if you look at other measures such as the amount of treatment being done, the numbers are still down, although not as steep as the fall in practice numbers.The government says that it is changing the dental contract and training more dentists in the areas most in need. The government says it will also make it a requirement for newly qualified dentists to practice in the NHS for a minimum period of at least three years.Campaign group 38 degrees calls the current dental crisis "shameful", with people being "forced to pay money they can't afford or suffer with the pain, shame, and further complications that come from being denied vital NHS healthcare".

schema.headline: How easy is it to find an NHS dentist? It depends on where you live

title: 'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents
description: Growing up in Manchester, Mia Tanswell didn't give her accent much thought - until her first week at university in Loughborough."I knew people were go
body: Growing up in Manchester, Mia Tanswell didn't give her accent much thought - until her first week at university in Loughborough."I knew people were going to notice that I was northern and that I didn't speak the 'Queen's English'," the 22-year-old says."Definitely in seminars I would sometimes feel like my accent would sound a bit less intellectual than other people, especially if I was the only northern student in the classroom."She's not alone. Fresh polling seen by the BBC suggests many workers still see so-called "accent bias" as a problem.The survey found one in 10 people in Britain feel anxious or self-conscious about their accent in high stakes professional settings such as speaking up in a business meeting.The research, conducted by the organisation More in Common of more than 3,300 adults across England, Scotland and Wales, found accent-related anxiety in work settings like these was highest among Geordies - from the region around Newcastle - and those with an east London - or Cockney - accent (at 19%), followed by people with a Welsh accent (at 18%).Around 5% of respondents believed their accent had cost them a promotion, pay rise or senior role. "Brummies" - people from Birmingham - were the most likely to feel this, at 13%.Respondents with a West Country accent reported the highest rate of having their accent mocked or criticised by colleagues, at 15%, followed by 13% of those with a Geordie accent.The poll was commissioned by Common Ground, an organisation which aims to promote social cohesion. Its founder, Lara Newman, has worked in construction, property and the built environment industry for more than 30 years, and says she changed her own accent to get ahead in the workplace."I am incredibly realistic about what would have happened had I gone to university or gone into the workplace with a strong west country accent," she says. "I felt like that was going to be an issue for me."Common Ground aims to support people from disadvantaged backgrounds into work but she says one of the layers creating a barrier to them is accent."I think there is a problem in the sense that [an accent] implies a level of education or otherwise. It implies class," she says.Most employers would say that is at least their ambition, to treat applicants and employees equally, regardless of their accent. Charlotte Davies, career expert at LinkedIn, says while there is still progress to be made "the direction of travel is encouraging"."Hiring is increasingly about skills, not background or polish. "Your accent is part of your story, and the workplaces getting this right, treat that as a strength, not something to smooth out," she says.Sian Jackson, a partner at law firm Mills & Reeve, says her company has recently changed its approach to encourage more local hiring and a diversity of accents."We don't judge, we scrutinise based on capability beyond somebody's accent, or appearance. Like any other prejudice or bias it's about being conscious of it so you can then set it aside," she says."We feel we've come a long way as a firm, but we are behind nationally compared to things like gender, so there is more progress to be made on accents."

schema.headline: 'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents
